name: Sleep hygiene basics

lead: Sleep hygiene is a set of habits meant to help sleep: regular times, a dark, cool, quiet bedroom, and limiting caffeine and alcohol late in the day. In looksmaxxing communities it is the foundational habit, on the belief that good sleep supports skin, the eye area and general appearance.

It aims to align behavior and environment with the body's sleep-wake rhythm and reduce arousal at bedtime. The concept was developed in the late 1970s for mild to moderate insomnia. Reviews describe the evidence that it alone improves sleep as weak, and a 2021 American Academy of Sleep Medicine meta-analysis did not favor it as stand-alone therapy for chronic insomnia.

paras: People set fixed bed and wake times, darken and cool the room, put screens away before bed, and cut caffeine and alcohol later in the day. It is usually the first layer before other sleep tools are added.
Little direct risk is reported. The AASM analysis cautioned that relying on it alone for chronic insomnia can delay effective treatment.

angle.text: A dark, cool, quiet and regular sleep routine is the baseline for better sleep quality and a more rested look in your skin and face. It was developed for mild to moderate insomnia.

lead: Sleep hygiene is a set of behavioral and environmental practices intended to promote healthy sleep, such as a regular schedule and a dark, cool, quiet bedroom. The concept was developed in the late 1970s to help people with mild to moderate insomnia.[1]
In looksmaxxing communities it is treated as a foundational habit, on the belief that good sleep supports skin, eye area and general appearance.[1]

Reviews describe the evidence that sleep hygiene alone improves sleep as weak and inconclusive, and a 2021 American Academy of Sleep Medicine meta-analysis did not favor it as stand-alone therapy for chronic insomnia.[1]
infobox: Peter Hauri, No More Sleepless Nights (1977)[1]
Fixed schedule; dark, cool, quiet room; limit caffeine and alcohol[1]

paras: Typical recommendations include waking at the same time daily, seeking bright light in the day and dim light before bed, exercising earlier, avoiding caffeine, nicotine and alcohol before bed, avoiding worry or work in bed, and keeping the bedroom quiet, dark and cool.[1]

Wikipedia traces early ideas to Paolo Mantegazza in 1864, the term to Willard Moyer in 1903, expansion by Nathaniel Kleitman in 1939, and Peter Hauri's 1977 book bringing it into sleep medicine. The 1990 International Classification of Sleep Disorders added inadequate sleep hygiene as a diagnosis, removed in the 2014 edition.[1]

Some items, such as avoiding noise, alcohol before bed and mentally demanding tasks before bed, have more support; others, such as comfortable mattresses or removing clocks, lack evidence. Following several recommendations together is linked to better outcomes, and combining education with cognitive behavioral therapy has improved insomnia in some studies.[1]

Critics in the literature note that studies use different sets of recommendations and that there is no evidence poor sleep hygiene causes insomnia; the AASM analysis warned that recommending it alone could delay effective treatment.[1][2]
A 2021 American Academy of Sleep Medicine meta-analysis did not favor sleep hygiene as stand-alone therapy for chronic insomnia.[1] No studies found on sleep hygiene and facial appearance.
